title: Thyroid function
subtitle: TSH and free T4 pattern recognition
summary: TSH and free T4 pattern recognition
introduction: Use laboratory-specific TSH and free T4 ranges. Acute illness, pregnancy, amiodarone, lithium, steroids, biotin and pituitary disease can alter interpretation.

rows.name: High TSH + low free T4
rows.referenceRange: RVH adult ranges: TSH 0.27–4.2 mIU/L; FT4 12–22 pmol/L
notes: Consider autoimmune thyroid disease, post-treatment disease or medication effects. Assess severity and symptoms rather than TSH alone.

rows.name: Low TSH + high free T4/T3
rows.referenceRange: RVH adult ranges: TSH 0.27–4.2 mIU/L; FT4 12–22 pmol/L; FT3 3.1–6.8 pmol/L
notes: Consider Graves disease, toxic nodules, thyroiditis or excessive replacement. Check pulse/rhythm, temperature, hydration and cardiovascular symptoms.

rows.name: High TSH + normal free T4
rows.referenceRange: RVH adult ranges: TSH 0.27–4.2 mIU/L; FT4 12–22 pmol/L
notes: Repeat and interpret with symptoms, thyroid antibodies, pregnancy plans and degree/persistence of TSH elevation.

rows.name: Low TSH + normal free T4/T3
rows.referenceRange: RVH adult ranges: TSH 0.27–4.2 mIU/L; FT4 12–22 pmol/L; FT3 3.1–6.8 pmol/L
notes: Consider medication, acute illness, pregnancy and early thyroid disease.

rows.name: Low/normal TSH + low free T4
rows.referenceRange: RVH adult ranges: TSH 0.27–4.2 mIU/L; FT4 12–22 pmol/L
notes: Do not label as primary hypothyroidism without considering pituitary disease, severe illness and medication effects.

urgentFindings: Possible thyroid storm: fever, marked tachycardia/AF, agitation/delirium, vomiting/diarrhoea, heart failure or shock.
Possible myxoedema coma: hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia or reduced consciousness.
New AF, chest pain, syncope or heart-failure features with biochemical hyperthyroidism.
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.

commonPatterns.title: Overt primary hypothyroidism
findings: Free T4 below the normal range
Fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation or bradycardia
interpretation: Consistent with primary hypothyroidism, commonly autoimmune (Hashimoto's), post-treatment (post-thyroidectomy/radioiodine) or medication-related
Severity should be judged on symptoms and physiology, not TSH alone — marked bradycardia, hypothermia or reduced consciousness raises concern for myxoedema coma
actions: Assess for red-flag features of myxoedema coma: hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, hypoventilation or reduced consciousness (see urgent findings)
Review medication (e.g. amiodarone, lithium) and biotin timing before attributing the result purely to thyroid disease
Arrange medical review for treatment initiation/titration if not already established on replacement

commonPatterns.title: Overt hyperthyroidism
findings: Free T4 and/or free T3 above the normal range
Tremor, weight loss, heat intolerance, palpitations or agitation
interpretation: Consistent with hyperthyroidism, for example Graves disease, toxic nodular disease, thyroiditis or excessive levothyroxine replacement
New AF, chest pain, syncope or heart-failure features alongside biochemical hyperthyroidism are time-critical, as is possible thyroid storm
actions: Check pulse and rhythm, temperature and cardiovascular symptoms, and obtain an ECG if AF or arrhythmia is suspected (see further testing)
Treat as time-critical if features of thyroid storm or new cardiac decompensation are present (see urgent findings)
Arrange medical review for further work-up (thyroid antibodies, cause) and treatment planning

commonPatterns.title: Subclinical hypothyroidism picture
findings: Free T4 within the normal range
interpretation: Represents a mild or early thyroid abnormality; management depends on the degree and persistence of TSH elevation, symptoms, thyroid antibody status and factors such as pregnancy planning, rather than a single result
actions: Repeat TSH/free T4 to confirm persistence before assuming this represents established disease
Consider thyroid antibodies where relevant to future risk (see further testing)
Arrange routine medical review rather than urgent escalation, unless there are symptoms warranting sooner assessment

commonPatterns.title: Subclinical hyperthyroidism picture
findings: Free T4 and free T3 within the normal range
interpretation: Consider early thyroid disease, medication effect or acute non-thyroidal illness; a low TSH is not always progressive thyrotoxicosis and often needs confirmation rather than immediate treatment
actions: Review medication list and recent acute illness as potential explanations before assuming underlying thyroid disease
Repeat testing to confirm persistence, particularly in older adults where subclinical hyperthyroidism carries AF and bone risk over time
Arrange routine medical review; escalate sooner if cardiac symptoms or AF are present (see urgent findings)

commonPatterns.title: Sick euthyroid / non-thyroidal illness pattern
findings: Low or low-normal TSH with low-normal or normal free T4/T3
Significant acute illness (e.g. sepsis, critical illness, major surgery)
interpretation: Acute illness commonly alters thyroid function tests without true thyroid disease being present ('sick euthyroid syndrome'); interpretation during acute illness is unreliable and can mimic central hypothyroidism
This pattern usually resolves as the underlying illness improves
actions: Avoid making a new diagnosis of thyroid disease from thyroid function tests taken during significant acute illness where possible
Repeat thyroid function after recovery from the acute illness if a genuine abnormality is still suspected
Focus management on treating the acute illness rather than the thyroid result in isolation

commonPatterns.title: Possible central (pituitary/hypothalamic) cause
findings: TSH low or inappropriately normal (not raised)
interpretation: A low free T4 without an appropriately raised TSH should not be labelled as primary hypothyroidism — it raises the possibility of pituitary or hypothalamic disease, severe non-thyroidal illness, or a medication effect
This distinction changes management and the need for wider pituitary assessment
actions: Review for other features of pituitary dysfunction (e.g. other hormone deficiencies, visual field change, headache) and recent severe illness or medication
Arrange medical review for further endocrine assessment rather than starting standard primary hypothyroidism treatment on this pattern alone
Do not delay treatment of an acutely unwell, hypotensive or hypoglycaemic patient while pursuing this distinction — consider adrenal insufficiency as a co-existing possibility

rationale: Supports confirmation of autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's or Graves) and helps predict progression in subclinical disease
Identifies atrial fibrillation or other arrhythmia associated with hyperthyroidism, and bradycardia associated with severe hypothyroidism
Hyponatraemia can occur with severe hypothyroidism/myxoedema coma and is part of the wider assessment of a systemically unwell patient with an abnormal thyroid picture
Hypoglycaemia is a feature of myxoedema coma and should be checked when this is suspected
Confirms whether a subclinical, sick-euthyroid or borderline pattern persists, improves or evolves before committing to a diagnosis or treatment
Adrenal insufficiency can co-exist with or mimic features of thyroid dysfunction in an acutely unwell patient and should be considered, particularly with hypotension or hypoglycaemia

specimens.notes: Plasma — green-top lithium-heparin tube with yellow insert, 3 mL. Biotin can interfere; RVH advises sampling no sooner than 8 hours after biotin administration.
